::: {.why}
A single average hides the conditional structure, and knowing which regimes each model wins in is more useful than knowing which won overall.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Report each model's performance conditional on volatility regime, on dispersion, and on sub-period.
- State whether the conditional pattern is stable enough to act on, using an interval rather than an eyeball.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [35 min]{.task-min} Run the conditional analysis: performance by volatility tercile, by cross-sectional dispersion tercile, and by sub-period, for every model, with intervals throughout. Then count how many conditional comparisons you have just made, since this is a place where conditioning can generate an apparent pattern out of nothing.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Test the pattern rather than describing it: if the flexible model appears to win in high-dispersion periods, check whether that holds in the validation period too. A conditional effect that appears only in the test period is a conditional effect you found by looking.
:::
:::

## Deliverable

::: {.deliverable}
Conditional performance by regime for every model with intervals, and a validation-period check on any conditional pattern found.
:::

## Checkpoint

::: {.checkpoint}
The boosting model wins in high-dispersion months. Is that real, and what did you do to find out?
:::
